title: Contributors
text:
The original AESZ database is/was hosted at Uni Mainz. The data for the AESZ database originates from the work of Gert Almkvist, Christian van Enckevort, Duco van Straten, Wadim Zudilin in https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0507430. The original online database was created by Pavel Metelitsyn.
The AESZ database has now been ported to the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in Bonn within the CYCluster project.
Contributors to the port of AESZ in CYCluster are:

Paul Blesse (Uni. Bonn)
Janis Duecker (Uni. Bonn)
Nutsa Gegelia (JGU Mainz)

title: Database API
text: This web site offers an application programming interface (API) which can be used to retrieve data programmatically with other programs for further processing. The API is based on PostgREST and documented in detail here.

title: Database API
text:
Basic usage
The API can be accessed over HTTPS and the basic structure of the URL is
/api/<table>?select=<field list>&<filter>
The only table available so far is operators, the list of Calabi-Yau operators (AESZ). The select part determines the columns to be shown in the output, the filter can be a combination of column names and conditions to narrow the set of displayed results.
When you search the AESZ table using the online form you can see (and copy) the corresponding API URL with filter at the foot of the results table.
Without the select part, all details about an operator are returned. Without the filter, all operators are returned.
For instance, /api/operators?nn=eq.4.3.1 returns all details about the operator with new number 4.3.1.
The query /api/operators?select=nn,operator_tex&degtheta=eq.2 lists new number and operator TeX of all operators with \theta-degree=2.

With curl in the terminal
A convenient way to access the API from a terminal and to store data locally to files, is using the curl download tool and optionally the jq JSON processor.
For instance, retrieve all details for the operator with new number 4.3.1 and save to a file:
curl '/api/operators?nn=eq.4.3.1' \
    | jq > op-4-3-1.json
Here jq will only pretty print the JSON data, but it could also be used for complicated filtering, processing and rewriting of the data.


With Python
In Python the requests library offers a simple way to retrieve JSON data, which can be processed with sympy:
import requests
import sympy

json = (requests
        .get("/api/operators?nn=eq.4.3.1")
        .json()[0])

z, theta, x = sympy.symbols("z theta X")

op = sum([ z**i * sympy.parse_expr(p, transformations='all')
           for i, p in enumerate(json['pols_list']) ])

print(op.subs(x,theta))
    


With Pari/GP
Pari cannot connect to web APIs directly, but we can call curl and jq as external programs. For instance, we can load the coefficients of the mirror map z(q) for operator 4.3.1 with:
zq = eval(externstr( \
   "curl -s '/api/operators?nn=eq.4.3.1' | " \
   "jq -r '.[0].zq_list | \"[\" + join(\", \") + \"]\"' ")[1])
Here jq is used to transform JSON data into a Pari compatible string that can be evaluated.


With Mathematica
In a Mathematica notebook run
operator = Association @ 
    Import["/api/operators?nn=eq.4.3.1"];

L = Total[MapIndexed[z^(#2[[1]] - 1)*#1 &, 
    ToExpression[operator["pols_list"]]]] /. X -> \[Theta]
    
instantons = ToExpression /@ operator["inst_list"]
to get a specific CY operator L. Other data can be accessed from the corresponding keyword, e.g., the list of instanton numbers.

title: CYCluster
text:
About
The new AESZ database provides arithmetic, algebraic, and enumerative information that complements the list of one-parameter Calabi–Yau operators compiled by Gert Almkvist, Christian van Enckevort, Duco van Straten, and Wadim Zudilin [1, 2].
The main additions are Euler factors of the Hasse–Weil zeta function, calculated following [3] to identify rank-two attractor points and test Langlands-type conjectures. Further additions include rational and integral monodromy structures.

title: CYCluster
text:
Related databases and software
Resources for the study of Calabi–Yau and Fano varieties.

Databases

Original AESZ database. The earlier database of Calabi–Yau differential operators.
L-functions and Modular Forms Database (LMFDB). Data on L-functions, modular forms, and related arithmetic objects.
Higher-genus invariants and Calabi–Yau data. Albrecht Klemm’s collection of data on Calabi–Yau threefolds and their enumerative invariants.
Quantum periods of four-dimensional Fano varieties. Data from Tom Coates and Alexander M. Kasprzyk.
Kreuzer–Skarke Calabi–Yau data. Max Kreuzer and Harald Skarke’s collections of 4,319 reflexive polytopes in dimension three and 473,800,776 in dimension four, including 30,108 distinct Hodge pairs for Calabi–Yau threefold hypersurface families.



Software tools

CYTools. Software from the Liam McAllister Group for studying Calabi–Yau manifolds, including triangulations and intersection numbers.
ore_algebra. Tools for analytic continuation of solutions of differential equations and computation of monodromy matrices.

Aufruf der Website

Art der Daten
Bei jedem Aufruf unserer Webseite erfassen unsere Server und Applikationen automatisiert Daten und Informationen vom System des aufrufenden Geräts.

Im Falle der Erfassung der Daten zur Bereitstellung der Website ist dies der Fall, wenn die jeweilige Sitzung beendet ist. Im Falle der Speicherung der Daten in Logfiles ist dies nach spätestens sieben Tagen der Fall. Eine darüberhinausgehende Speicherung ist möglich.
